outline.description: Introduces the defendants, the alleged social-media-based pump-and-dump scheme, and the charges brought under the federal securities fraud statutes.
subtopics: Defendants’ identities and large social-media followings
Alleged pump-and-dump mechanics: buy, post false/misleading statements to induce purchases, secretly sell
Nature of the misrepresentations: trading positions and potential price of securities
Alleged profits from the scheme (approximately $114 million)
Counts charged: conspiracy to commit securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349) and substantive securities fraud (18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 & 2)

outline.chapter_title: Procedural History and Standard of Review
outline.description: Explains how the case reached the Fifth Circuit, what the district court decided, and the standard for assessing the sufficiency of an indictment.
subtopics: District court dismissal for failure to state an offense (no deprivation of a traditional property interest)
Government’s timely appeal
De novo review of indictment sufficiency
Taking indictment’s allegations as true at the motion-to-dismiss stage
Indictment sufficiency requirements: enumerate each element, fair notice, and double-jeopardy protection

outline.chapter_title: Governing Law: Securities Fraud under § 1348 and Its Mail/Wire Fraud Roots
outline.description: Sets out the elements of securities fraud, how § 1348 borrows from mail and wire fraud, and the role of recent Supreme Court precedent.
subtopics: § 1348 elements: scheme to defraud and intent to defraud
Borrowing concepts from mail and wire fraud jurisprudence
Scheme to defraud: material misrepresentation intended to obtain something of value
Intent to defraud: intent to deceive and to cause some harm from the deceit
Kousisis formulation: deception plus obtaining money or property as an object of the scheme

outline.chapter_title: Issue One: Scheme to Defraud and the Property Interest Requirement
outline.description: Analyzes whether the indictment alleges a deprivation of money or property, distinguishing the rejected right-to-control theory from the valid fraudulent-inducement theory.
subtopics: Defendants’ argument: indictment alleges only deprivation of valuable economic information
Ciminelli: right-to-control theory invalid because it targets non-traditional property interests
Fraudulent-inducement theory (Kousisis): using misstatements to induce transfer of money or property
Application: allegations that followers were induced to buy securities—parting with money—fit fraudulent inducement, not right-to-control
Conclusion: indictment adequately alleges a scheme to defraud of money/property

outline.chapter_title: Issue Two: Intent to Defraud and Whether Harm Must Be Alleged
outline.description: Addresses whether the indictment must allege intended economic harm, explaining why profiting via deception suffices even if victims receive market-value securities.
subtopics: Defendants’ argument: intent to profit, not to harm; no victim loss alleged
Kousisis: fraud complete upon scheming to obtain victim’s money or property, regardless of net loss
Application: alleged posts designed to induce purchases show intent to obtain money via deceit
Receiving market-value securities does not negate fraud liability
Reinforcement: no mirror-image loss/gain requirement; obtaining money was an object of the scheme

outline.description: Summarizes the court’s holding and outlines the opinion’s implications for securities fraud prosecutions, especially those involving social media and post-Ciminelli/Kousisis charging theories.
subtopics: Holding: indictment sufficiently alleges scheme and intent to defraud; reversal of dismissal and remand
What proceeds on remand: case returns for further criminal proceedings on the merits
Charging guidance: avoid right-to-control framing; plead fraudulent inducement to obtain money/property
Practical import for social-media pump-and-dump cases: misrepresentations that induce purchases can satisfy § 1348
Doctrinal takeaway: post-Kousisis, intent-to-harm-as-net-loss is unnecessary when obtaining money/property is an object
